newsitem.title: USA: US Comptroller won't automatically recuse himself.
newsitem.headline: US Comptroller won't automatically recuse himself.

text.p: U.S. Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig told lawmakers Thursday he will not automatically recuse himself from rulings involving banks whose executives attended a controversial White House Coffee meeting last year.
"I do not believe that simply coming to a coffee is a matter that would warrant recusal," Ludwig told members of the Senate Banking Committee's Financial Institutions Subcommittee.

Last month, Ludwig recused himself from consideration of a historic request from NationsBank Corp for expanded powers, fearing his participation in the decision would be tainted by a NationsBank executive's attendance at the controversial White House meeting last May that was organized by the Democratic National Committee.
"I would not intend to do so solely on that basis. What I am required to do is look at all the facts and circumstances," Ludwig told Senator Richard Shelby.
But Shelby, an Alabama Republican, asked whether or not Ludwig's moves are enough to clear any potential conflicts of interest.
"How do we know up here on the Banking Committee that the NationsBank applications are not just an eye and a wink?" Shelby asked.

Ludwig defended his actions, adding that any other potential conflicts would have to be determined on a case-by-case basis. "I try to maintain the highest level of integrity standards," Ludwig assured the panel.
"The standard doesn't look very high, it looks pretty low today," Shelby said.

Ludwig also faced tough questions from members of the Senate Panel about his agency's approval last year of rules that would allow banks, through subsidiaries, to engage in an array of non-banking businesses, including insurance underwriting.
Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, faulted the agency for adopting the rules, saying such regulatory relief should first have been dealt with by Congress.
"You have made it even more difficult," D'Amato said.
